title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning
claim: Matching data across paired evaluations cancels oracle noise, while mismatched evaluation amplifies variance as the perturbation scale shrinks.
layout: 1 log-log line plot, shaded gap with bracket annotation, legend top-right
description: A single log-log line chart. The x-axis is perturbation scale μ, running from 10^-4 to 10^-2. The y-axis is dimension-normalized oracle-noise variance V(μ), from 10^-2 to 10^6. Two overlapping lines slope steeply downward from the top left to the right. One is a red dashed line with squares for BOLT-mismatch. The other is a gold dashed line with triangles for on-policy RL. A gray label next to them reads 'predicted ∝ μ^-2'. A blue line with circles for BOLT-match stays flat near 2e-2, with the note '≈ constant'. A pale blue shaded region fills the gap between the curves. A vertical gray bracket at the left edge is labeled '~10^8× lower'. The legend sits in the top right. The eye goes first to the large gap between the red/gold lines and the blue line.
caption: Oracle-noise variance across perturbation scales. Matched BOLT remains nearly constant, while mismatched BOLT and on-policy RL follow the predicted 1/µ2 trend. Both axes are logarithmic.
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliability in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/Î¼^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $Î¼$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results motivate the ZO-BOLT algorithm, which builds on BOLT's matched-data advantage for reliable ZO optimization of an RLVR-aligned objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three models and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.
